input: Teach my kids to ride bikes

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The number of kids, their ages, and current ability levels completely changes the teaching approach — a 4-year-old needs balance-bike progressions while a 9-year-old might just need stabiliser removal and a confidence boost.
What counts as success matters for planning: is the goal first solo pedal strokes, steering confidently, or riding independently on roads? This defines how many sessions are needed.
Available time — whether this is a single weekend push or spread over several weeks — dictates session length, pacing, and how much can be covered per day.
The location (quiet car park, garden, park path) affects safety, surface type, and what drills are practical. An incline or grass vs. tarmac changes technique.
Whether appropriate bikes and safety gear (helmet, knee pads) are already owned or need to be sourced is a prerequisite before any teaching can start.
Some kids respond to structured step-by-step drills; others need play-based, low-pressure exposure. Knowing the child's temperament shapes how lessons should feel and be framed.
Understanding what the parent considers 'done well' — e.g., riding solo 50 metres, turning, stopping safely — ensures the plan has a clear finish line and avoids overplanning or underplanning.

gold.taskTitle: Teach my kids to ride bikes
gold.taskDescription: Plan and carry out a process to get the kids independently riding bikes.

questions.title: How old is each child, and can they balance at all?
questions.description: Capture the age and current skill level of every child involved so the teaching method can be matched appropriately.

questions.title: What should each child be able to do by the end?
questions.description: Define the finish-line skill — first solo pedal strokes, riding 50+ metres, turning, stopping — so the plan has a clear target.

questions.title: How much time do you have to dedicate to this?
questions.description: Establish whether this is a single-weekend effort or spread across multiple weeks, and how long each session can realistically be.

questions.title: Where will the lessons take place?
questions.description: Identify the specific location — garden, quiet car park, park path — to account for surface, space, and safety when designing drills.

questions.title: Do the kids already have bikes and helmets that fit?
questions.description: Confirm whether correctly sized bikes and essential safety gear are already available or need to be bought or borrowed first.

questions.title: How does each child react to trying new, challenging things?
questions.description: Understand each child's temperament — cautious, fearless, easily frustrated — so lessons can be framed in a way that keeps them motivated.

questions.title: Should the plan cover one child at a time or both together?
questions.description: Clarify whether the parent wants to teach the children simultaneously or in separate focused sessions, as this changes structure and supervision needs.
